articles.title: The year’s weirdest game is hard to explain and even harder to put down
articles.summary: Titanium Court, a new indie game from developer AP Thomson, is a strange mixture of genres that’s available now on Steam.
articles.body: The first rule of Titanium Court is that you can’t explain Titanium Court. Not because we’re living under the omerta of an 8-bit Fight Club, but because it’s one truth I can stand by. For the past week, I’ve been facing the consequences of getting isekai’d into a digital pastiche of the entire history of dramatic allegory and contemporary humor, leading a whimsical quasi-sentient court of wildly unmedicated faeries to their doom. They try, in their roundabout faerie way, to be helpful, because I don’t know what I’m doing. “I’m looking forward to you explaining the game to me,” said my editor Andrew Webster — words he silently swallowed after I tried to do just that. This isn’t to say that Titanium Court is unknowable. It is simply one of those things you have to experience for yourself. The most straightforward description, to paraphrase from developer AP Thomson’s game credits, is “a match-3 tower defense game for people who love to read.” This is a bit of an understatement because Titanium Court is also a point-and-click roguelite RPG, a resource management game, a deckbuilder, a visual novel metacomedy of manners, a whole helping of postmodern theater, an ode to HyperCard, the equivalent of ludic ASMR for appreciators of the victory animation from Windows 98 Solitaire, and, if you grew up reading Norton Juster’s The Phantom Tollbooth, Titanium Court is a rare and precious gift. We begin with literal curtains parting and an emcee stepping forward with an introduction. He discusses my role as the player with the nonchalance of a zookeeper giving a tour of the lion enclosure at feeding time. And just like that, we begin with the player minding their own business — a blip of pixels moving through a gridded landscape — before the entire map trembles and reforms to introduce the mechanics and key components of the terrain that you can “harvest” by matching at least three tiles (wheat gives food, hills give stone, and so on). Soon, over the horizon, we see the mysterious Court and are swept inside to meet its faerie residents. Here, the world lives at the mercy of a magic tide, with no clear way of leaving. [Media: There are two modes: when you’re at war, and when you’re not. Being at war is a deeply unserious yet profound endeavor – the Court is immortal, so death isn’t really a huge deal to them, but you also can’t get a grip on the Court’s absurd mythology and the faeries’ evasiveness. War is matter-of-fact and routine. It’s something you wake up and do after breakfast, which involves choosing a job (the default is as the Monarch, which earns money per enemy keep destroyed), and learning to traverse two kinds of maps, strategize between different terrain and enemies, and find different ways to overcome bosses. My favorite job is Youth, which you receive by means of a cigarette lighter and involves incinerating tiles on the board to make money. Every battle begins with High Tide — the match-3 portion — where you do your best to arrange the board to your advantage. Low Tide is when the RPG / combat / management stuff kicks in. You queue up workers and combat units, make transactions with vendors, and take advantage of useful buildings like hospitals and shops. Sometimes you might find a giant jar, or come across a man on a stump, or float past a billboard that captures the imagination of the Court (faeries do not believe in cars, and every time you see a road sign designed for vehicular laws, it causes a small fuss). You might try an obscure solution from a magic journal entry you can’t remember writing, gleaned from a hallucinated future in which you are a clockwork monastery. Once everything is arranged how you want it, hit the play button, sit back, and hope for the best: All your little dudes stream out of the Court in a queue, perform their duties on a set timer, and hopefully, the Court remains standing when time is up. If all goes well you win the battle and edge closer to the boss on the overworld map. If not, you get wine and “comfort.” After enough progress, you are offered the chance to skip boss fights by watching a wholly unskippable musical performance by AP Thomson himself, rendered in grainy, nigh-indecipherable full-motion video. The first one I watched was — and I say this with the utmost admiration for everyone involved — like if Paul Banks from Interpol was in Ween and did an educational take on the Salmon Dance. I realize it sounds like I have a gas leak in my apartment, but I don’t. I have something better, which is Titanium Court. [Image: When you aren’t at war, you’re hanging around the Court, an arcane medieval keep as befits a bunch of meddling faeries, but with the blessing of modern plumbing. The faeries here are a decidedly magical but contemporary bunch who believe in science and alcohol and supporting their beloved queen, even when it hurts them. There are curses and secret rooms and arguments to be settled. There is sportsball and a library and a cat. There’s a lot to unpack within the Court’s walls about why you were brought here, what you need to do, and how you leave, both allegorically and mechanically. Every night, everything collapses, and the next morning, it begins anew. Titanium Court doesn’t break the fourth wall; it makes the player dismantle it themselves, brick by brick, before leaving them there in a limbo of indecisive regret and sentimental reflection, perhaps to build a new outlook of their own. The Court isn’t just a place. It’s an exercise in self-restraint and self-gratification, brimming with wordplay and satire and the endless “yes, and” mentality of good improv. At one point, after hours of (extremely good and creatively wrought) misdirection, after hours of NPCs trying to both help and hinder me, the game threw me such an emotional curveball that I had to step away and hug my cat. It dawned on me that AP Thomson is Jigsaw. He is squatting behind the scenes with his guitar, cackling when I realize the effect I’m having on the faeries as I hit the 15-hour mark of playtime. Maybe the real game is trying to explain Titanium Court and failing, and in the process realizing what it’s done to your understanding of capital-m Magic — the silvery intangible stuff that glues our imagination together. When I finally manage to leave the Court, I marvel at having somehow survived all these deeply personal surgical strikes not just on me as a player, but on my relationship with storytelling and fiction as a whole. It’s a singular metacomedy that learned how to layer its story beats from the best sitcoms, and plays out like your most correct frenemy telling you exactly what you don’t want to hear about the nature of consumerism and entertainment. This is the sort of game that will undoubtedly launch a thousand discussions, but for me it will remain personal and private. Nobody needs to know how much suffering I caused before I got up and walked away. To understand what that means, you’ll have to play it for yourself. Titanium Court launches April 23rd on Steam.

articles.standfirst: Os clientes concorrerão a 1.225 prêmios e vales-compra de R$ 500,00 e R$ 1.000,00 e certificados em barras de ouro nos valores de R$ 20.000,00, de R$ 100.000,00 e de R$ 400.000,00.
articles.summary: Os clientes concorrerão a 1.225 prêmios e vales-compra de R$ 500,00 e R$ 1.000,00 e certificados em barras de ouro nos valores de R$ 20.000,00, de R$ 100.000,00 e de R$ 400.000,00.
articles.body:
Promoção “Festival da Sorte Tauste” — Foto: Crédito: Divulgação.

O Tauste Supermercados iniciou na sexta-feira, 18 de setembro, a Promoção “Festival da Sorte Tauste”, que distribuirá 1.225 prêmios, no valor total de R$ 2,56 milhões.

Entre os prêmios estão 960 vales-compra de R$ 500,00, 240 vales-compra de R$ 1.000,00, 12 certificados em barras de ouro no valor de R$ 20 mil cada, equivalentes às motos, e 12 certificados em barras de ouro de R$ 100 mil cada, equivalentes aos carros, além do grande prêmio final, um certificado em barras de ouro no valor de R$ 400 mil, equivalente a casa.

A promoção será válida para compras realizadas nas 12 lojas Tauste, localizadas em Marília, Bauru, Sorocaba, Jundiaí, São José dos Campos, Campinas, Taubaté e São Paulo, além do Tauste Delivery e do Restaurante e Pizzaria La Dirna.

Para participar, é necessário estar cadastrado no Clube Tauste e informar o CPF no ato da compra. A cada R$ 70 em compras, o cliente recebe um Número da Sorte. A Promoção é válida para as lojas físicas, para o Tauste Delivery e para o Restaurante e Pizzaria La Dirna.

O período de participação é de 18 de Setembro de 2026 a 14 de Janeiro de 2027, com sorteios realizados com base nas extrações da Loteria Federal. Os números da sorte são gerados automaticamente e podem ser consultados no site oficial da campanha: .

A Promoção Festival da Sorte Tauste terá uma nova dinâmica para os sorteios, a fim de ampliar as oportunidades de contemplação. Serão realizados sorteios ao longo da Campanha com contemplação em todas as lojas da rede, aumentando as chances dos clientes em cada cidade.

Ao final da Promoção, o sorteio do prêmio principal será válido para todos os clientes da rede no período de participação.

Os nomes dos contemplados e respectivos Números da Sorte serão divulgados no site oficial e nos canais de comunicação do Tauste em até cinco dias úteis após cada apuração.

A promoção “Festival da Sorte Tauste” é autorizada pela Secretaria de Prêmios e Apostas do Ministério da Fazenda (SPA/MF), por meio do Certificado de Autorização SPA/ME nº 04.052427/2026. O regulamento completo está disponível no site oficial do Clube Tauste.

articles.title: ‘Jailer 2’ Preview: Rajinikanth returns as Tiger Muthuvel Pandian with new enemies, bigger stakes and more action
articles.summary: Superstar Rajinikanth has broken his no-sequel rule for the much awaited ‘Jailer 2’ helmed by Nelson Dilipkumar.
articles.body: Superstar Rajinikanth has broken his no-sequel rule for the much awaited ‘Jailer 2’ helmed by Nelson Dilipkumar. With the second part set to hit the big screens tomorrow on October 15, let's take a look at what to expect from the film, as the legendary star is back as Tiger Muthuvel Pandian who is dragged into the violence yet again.Written and directed by Nelson Dilipkumar, the sequel continues the story of the retired jailer who was pulled back into the underworld after his son’s apparent murder in the first film. This time the dangerous world is back with new enemies and bigger stakes.Trailer of Rajinikanth’s ‘Jailer 2’In the trailer we saw Rajinikanth’s character Muthuvel Pandian is introduced to a new threat through Suraj Venjaramoodu’s character, Dileep, who is seen interrogating someone about a man they are trying to find. The sequence suggests that Muthuvel is being hunted.However, the trailer reveals that Muthuvel has not gone into hiding. Instead, he has taken up the identity of an ordinary car driver, using another disguise to stay under the radar.We also see some new faces joining the franchise as the trailer show, S J Suryah’s Bodhi Kalpak also appears as a major threat. He challenges Muthuvel’s methods and asks, “Can only the Jailer set up snipers? Why wouldn't I?”The trailer also introduces Vidya Balan’s Kantha, who offers Muthuvel tea or coffee. When he refuses, she responds, “You can only choose between tea or coffee. You can't choose whether you're willing to drink it or not.”The sequel is expected to explore whether Muthuvel is forced back into violence or chooses to confront the new threat himself.Faces of ‘Jailer 2’Talking about the cast, Rajinikanth returns as Tiger Muthuvel Pandian, alongside Ramya Krishnan as his wife, Vijaya Pandian. Mirnaa reprises her role as Swetha Pandian, Arjun’s widow, while Rithvik returns as Muthuvel’s grandson. Yogi Babu is also back as Vimal, the local taxi driver.The film also brings back several popular characters from the first instalment. Mohanlal returns as Matthew, an underworld figure and Muthuvel’s trusted ally. Shiva Rajkumar reprises his role as Narasimha, while Jackie Shroff returns as Kamdev, the gangster who eventually becomes Muthuvel’s ally.The new cast also includes Suraj Venjaramoodu, Mithun Chakraborty and Apeksha Porwal. Apeksha appears in the trailer performing action sequences with a gun. Nora Fatehi has also been announced for a special dance number titled Bindaas, while reports suggest that Vijay Sethupathi and Hrithik Roshan may appear in cameos.Why did Rajinikanth agree to do a sequel?During the promotional event of ‘Jailer 2’, Rajinikanth also explained why he agreed to return for a sequel despite generally preferring standalone films. “I usually don’t prefer sequels. I feel like whatever is in Part 1, they’ll add salt and spices to it. I was approached for Baasha 2 and Petta 2, but I did not agree to do them,” he said.He explained that the first film left enough story possibilities for another instalment, particularly through Varman’s criminal network and the containers worth Rs. 1,000 crore revealed towards the end.Talking about the technical team, Anirudh Ravichander returns as the music composer, while Vijay Kartik Kannan handles cinematography and R. Nirmal takes care of editing.‘Jailer 2’ arrives in theatres worldwide on October 15, 2026 in multiple languages.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Neetu Kapoor recalls sangeet night where Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan performed and Rishi Kapoor couldn't stop appreciating him: 'Rarest of the rare'
articles.summary: Neetu Kapoor recently took a trip down memory lane, sharing a rare glimpse from her wedding celebrations with late husband Rishi Kapoor.
articles.body: Neetu Kapoor recently took a trip down memory lane, sharing a rare glimpse from her wedding celebrations with late husband Rishi Kapoor. The actor posted a throwback photograph from their sangeet night on Instagram, capturing a special moment featuring legendary Pakistani singer Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan.The photograph shows Nusrat performing at Rishi Kapoor’s residence, with the late actor seen enjoying and appreciating the singer’s soulful rendition. Describing the moment as “Rarest of the rare. Rishi ji appreciating Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan,” the image brought back memories of the couple’s wedding festivities. Neetu captioned her post, “Our sangeet night,” accompanied by two pink heart emojis.Rishi Kapoor and Neetu Singh tied the knot on January 22, 1980, at RK House in Chembur. While their wedding was a grand affair, Neetu later revealed that the celebrations were so crowded that both she and Rishi struggled to cope with the situation.During an appearance on Swiggy’s YouTube channel, the actor recalled how she fainted amid the crowds, while Rishi, who was afraid of crowds, also passed out before mounting a horse for the ceremony.“I fainted because there were too many people, and my husband was petrified of crowds, so before getting onto the horse he fainted. So he was having brandy. I was having brandy. So that's how our wedding was, I was drunk when I was taking the pheras," she said.Neetu also shared an unusual anecdote from the wedding, revealing that the large gathering had attracted pickpockets who managed to blend in with the guests. Some even presented the couple with bizarre gifts.“There were pickpockets at my wedding. They gave me gifts that had stones, chappals. They were all so well dressed and we thought they were guests. They crashed the wedding because it was such a huge wedding,” Neetu recalled.Rishi Kapoor passed away on April 30, 2020, at the age of 67. The veteran actor died at Sir H. N. Reliance Foundation Hospital in Mumbai after battling leukaemia for two years.On the work front, Neetu Kapoor was last seen in the family comedy-drama ‘Daadi Ki Shaadi’, which arrived in theatres on May 8.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: 'Drishyam 3’ director Abhishek Pathak rules out ‘Drishyam 4’, says Ajay Devgn, Shriya Saran and Tabu starrer thriller has reached a ‘beautiful ending’: ‘Let’s not spoil it’
articles.summary: Director Abhishek Pathak has ruled out the possibility of a fourth instalment of the Ajay Devgn-led 'Drishyam' franchise, maintaining that 'Drishyam 3:
articles.body: Director Abhishek Pathak has ruled out the possibility of a fourth instalment of the Ajay Devgn-led 'Drishyam' franchise, maintaining that 'Drishyam 3: The Conclusion' marks the end of Vijay Salgaonkar’s story. Despite the crime thriller’s strong theatrical run and growing audience interest in another sequel, Pathak believes the latest film provides a fitting conclusion to the much-loved franchise.Abhishek Pathak explains why ‘Drishyam 3’ is the final chapterIn an interview with SCREEN, Pathak expressed hope that October 2 would continue to be celebrated as Drishyam Day, while reiterating that the team considers the third instalment the franchise’s final chapter. He emphasised that another film cannot be made simply because audiences want one, as the story must justify its continuation.“All of us believe this is the last part of the film. Obviously, the audience is loving it and talking about it. But 'Drishyam' isn’t the franchise where we can just decide to make another film. It’s very much dependent on the story, and the story has ended. I always thought the ending was very poetic. It’s a love letter to the franchise,” he said.Fans want ‘Drishyam 4’, but the director wants to preserve the endingPathak acknowledged that several people have approached him with the possibility of a fourth instalment, pointing out that the franchise’s premise could potentially offer more narrative avenues. However, he believes the existence of further story possibilities is not, by itself, a reason to extend the franchise.“The closure is beautifully done. That’s what people liked about it. A lot of people are telling me there can be a part 4. If you get to it, there can be enormous amount of story to it, but that’s not the point,” the director said.He further explained that the team had to bring the story to a close at some point and felt the third film offered the right ending. With 'Drishyam 3' still drawing audiences to cinemas, Pathak urged the team and fans to appreciate the conclusion rather than push for another sequel.“We had to stop it at some point, and this was a beautiful ending to the franchise. 'Drishyam 3' is only in its second week right now. People are still coming to theatres in huge numbers. The second weekend was more than Rs 60 crore. That’s a figure too many films don’t achieve even in their lifetime. So, let’s not spoil it for them,” he added.What is ‘Drishyam 3: The Conclusion’ about?The latest instalment brings Ajay Devgn back as Vijay Salgaonkar, a man whose carefully guarded secrets come under threat once again when a determined Crime Branch officer reopens the case. Tabu, Shriya Saran, Ishita Dutta and Jaideep Ahlawat also feature in pivotal roles.The film has also received praise from Malayalam superstar Mohanlal, who headlined the original Malayalam 'Drishyam' franchise. Congratulating the team, he expressed appreciation for the way the Hindi instalment concluded its story.“I watched 'Drishyam: The Conclusion', and I am truly impressed with the way they have brought this much-loved journey to a befitting end. Congratulations to Abhishek Pathak, Kumar Mangat Pathak, Ajay Devgn, and the entire cast and crew on a job so well done,” he said.‘Drishyam 3’ continues its record-breaking box office run'Drishyam 3: The Conclusion' has emerged as one of the biggest box office successes of 2026. According to Sacnilk, the film collected Rs 501.80 crore worldwide in its first 12 days, including Rs 323.50 crore in India net collections. It opened with Rs 62 crore on its first day and went on to earn Rs 245.50 crore during its opening week.A strong second weekend further boosted its collections, helping the film become the highest-grossing title of Ajay Devgn’s career. It has also secured the position of the second highest-grossing Indian film of 2026, surpassing the reported lifetime collections of ‘Border 2,’ ‘Toxic,’ ‘Jana Nayagan’ and ‘Peddi.'Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Quote of the day by Kelly Clarkson: ‘It’s ignorant to think you know everything about person, there are just different colors to personality,' lesson on individuality and complex human nature by the ‘Breakaway’ singer
articles.summary: Kelly Clarkson shares a powerful message about individuality, emphasizing that it is ignorant to think you know everything about a person due to their complex personalities. Discover her thoughts on understanding human nature and the multifaceted aspects of each individual.
articles.body: Kelly Clarkson has been a reckoning force in the music industry since the early 2000s. From ‘Breakaway’ to ‘Stronger’ and ‘Since You’ve Been Gone,' the star has worked on a lot of chart-topping numbers. Over the years, speaking from experience, Clarkson shared her thoughts on how everyone is different and that they cannot be judged just based on one instance since human beings are far more complex than that.The quote of the day by the famed singer reads, "It's ignorant to think you know everything about a person. There are many different sides to everybody's personality, and there are just different colors to a personality.”What does the quote from Kelly Clarkson mean?Kelly Clarkson said this line during a behind-the-scenes featurette for her ‘Mr. Know It All’ music video in late August 2011.The quote from the famed singer is all about understanding the concepts of snap judgments, assumptions, and superficial labeling. Inherently, she is talking about understanding the fact that every single person is unique in their own ways, and no single interaction, reputation, or public image can be the true definition of who a person is.Believing you completely understand someone, whether it be a celebrity, partner, coworker, or enemy, is a form of arrogance, and something that is not possible. People usually tend to pass judgement on others based on a specific thing or a behavior they observed in a specific context. The quote warns that assuming the part equals the whole is a misjudgment and inherently wrong.People are multi-faceted and have different personalities and traits, and there are a lot of different sides to an individual. People adapt based on where they are and who they are with. Someone who is stoic at work might be deeply emotional at home; someone who seems guarded on stage may be deeply open with close friends. Human nature is inherently complex and contradictory. A person can be strong and vulnerable, confident and insecure, serious and goofy, and reducing someone to a single thing strips away their humanity.At the end of the day, Clarkson’s quote is all about understanding that we need to stay curious about people rather than assuming we've got them all figured out. It also serves as a reminder that public figures, celebrities, and online personalities present curated snapshots, not their whole lives, and what they show on social media cannot be the only thing that may be used to define who they are. Clarkson also encourages us to accept our own complexity and that it’s okay to show different sides of ourselves in different seasons of life and let ourselves be vulnerable to the people around us.About Kelly Clarkson’s early lifeKelly Brianne Clarkson was born on April 24, 1982, in Fort Worth, Texas, and grew up in nearby Burleson and was the youngest of three siblings. Her mother, Jeanne Ann, was a first-grade English teacher, while her father, Stephen Michael Clarkson, was a former engineer. She was raised in a Southern Baptist household in the small city of Burleson, Texas.When Clarkson was six years old, her parents filed for divorce. The split resulted in her brother going to live with their father, her sister going to stay with an aunt, and Kelly staying in Burleson with her mother. She started honing her singing skills in school when her middle school choir teacher, Cynthia Glenn, heard Clarkson singing to herself in a hallway and encouraged her to audition for the school choir. On her encouragement, she joined the choir and continued singing through high school. Not only that, but she also started performing in school musicals such as 'Brigadoon,' ‘Seven Brides for Seven Brothers,' and ‘Annie Get Your Gun.'She graduated in 2000 and right off the bat was offered full music scholarships to several universities, which included the University of Texas at Austin, North Texas State, and Berklee College of Music. However, Clarkson declined all of them since she wished to dive straight into pursuing a full-time recording career.About Kelly Clarkson’s career in music and rise to global stardomClarkson started her career by doing odd jobs such as cocktail waitressing, working at a movie theater, telemarketing, and promoting Red Bull to make ends meet while she focused on her music career. She moved to Los Angeles in 2001 to support her music career and even landed roles in television shows like ‘Sabrina the Teenage Witch.' When her LA home burned down, she ended up broke and without a home and had to move back to Burleson, Texas. Shortly after returning home in 2002, her friends encouraged her to audition for the inaugural season of a new reality television singing competition: ‘American Idol,' and the rest is history.She was the first winner of the TV show, and it all kickstarted her career into the music industry. Over the years, Clarkson has been well known for her powerhouse vocals and her soulful pop music. According to Celebrity Net Worth, the star now has a net worth of USD 600 million, with an annual salary of USD 16 million. After signing a record deal, she released ‘A Moment Like This,' which reached number 1 on the Billboard 200 charts, and most of her work that followed went high up on the charts.Over the course of her career, Kelly Clarkson has won 3 Grammy Awards out of 17 total nominations. Some of her other wins include 8 wins out of 15+ nominations for Daytime Emmy Awards, 4 AMA awards, 2 Academy of Country Music Awards, and a star in the Hollywood Walk of Fame, which was awarded to her in 2022.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Nana Patekar prayer meet: Shivaji Satam, Rohini Hattangadi, Sanjay Jadhav and others pay tribute to the late actor in Mumbai
articles.summary: Veteran actor Nana Patekar passed away on Thursday, October 8, 2026, at the age of 75, following a cardiac arrest at his residence in Dona Paula, Goa.
articles.body: Veteran actor Nana Patekar passed away on Thursday, October 8, 2026, at the age of 75, following a cardiac arrest at his residence in Dona Paula, Goa. His demise marked the loss of one of Indian cinema's most distinctive performers, whose career spanned Hindi and Marathi films, theatre and socially driven initiatives. Known for his intense screen presence and memorable performances, the actor has left behind a legacy that continues to resonate with audiences and the film fraternity.Shivaji Satam, Sanjay Jadhav and others attend prayer meetA prayer meet titled ‘Aathvanilya Nana’, with the accompanying Marathi inscription ‘Swargiya Nana Patekar yancha smrutina ujala’, is being held at the P.L. Deshpande Maharashtra Kala Academy complex in Prabhadevi, Mumbai, in memory of the late actor. Several personalities from the Marathi film industry, including actors Shivaji Satam and Rohini Hattangadi, filmmaker Sanjay Jadhav and director Mehul Kumar, have attended the gathering to pay their respects. The meet offers colleagues, friends and admirers an opportunity to remember the actor's contribution to Indian cinema and Marathi theatre.A special rangoli drawn at the entrance of the venue has also caught attention. The artwork featured Nana Patekar's character from his iconic Marathi film 'Natsamrat', serving as a visual tribute to one of his most celebrated performances.Nana Patekar's funeral held with full state honoursEarlier, Nana Patekar's last rites were performed on October 8 at his farmhouse in Donje village near Khadakwasla, in Pune district. The actor was cremated with full state honours in recognition of his immense contribution to Indian cinema and theatre. Family members, friends, film personalities and political leaders gathered to bid him farewell. His funeral also drew admirers who remembered him not only for his acting but also for his association with farmers and social welfare initiatives.Nana Patekar's final films to release after his demiseAlthough Nana Patekar is no longer among us, audiences may still see some of his performances on screen through projects awaiting release. His reported upcoming releases include 'Shakti Shalini', featuring Aneet Padda; the Marathi biographical drama 'Eetha', inspired by the life of celebrated Lavani performer Vithabai Narayangaonkar; and 'Vedantam' and 'Kuku Ki Kundali'. 'The Confession of Mary', which premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival, is also among his recent projects.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Harry Styles challenged by GOP gov candidate to put migrant shot by ICE ‘on his tour bus’ after MSG tribute
articles.summary: New York GOP gubernatorial nominee Bruce Blakeman ripped Harry Styles as "out-of-touch" after the singer honored a migrant shot by ICE during a recent performance at MSG.
articles.body: New York GOP gubernatorial nominee Bruce Blakeman decried Harry Styles as an "out-of-touch" elitist after the singer paid tribute at his Madison Square Garden performance to a migrant shot during a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operation. "I think Harry Styles should put that guy on his tour bus and tour around the country with this guy, who is a convicted criminal," he said Tuesday on "Fox & Friends." "He is alleged to have gang activity. He's alleged to be involved in drug-dealing poison to our children." Styles, who is doing a 30-night residency at Madison Square Garden, took a moment during his show to honor 28-year-old Oscar Belgal, a migrant from the Dominican Republic who was shot by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on Thursday while his 5-year-old son was in the back seat of the car. HARRY STYLES ADDRESSES ICE SHOOTING IN NEW YORK WITH CALL FOR ‘DIGNITY AND JUSTICE’ "I just want us to take a moment to think about Oscar Belgal tonight, and I want us to just think and remember to just look after each other," the singer said. Blakeman criticized Styles over the tribute, arguing that illegal immigrants with prior convictions should be deported and not defended by celebrities. "It's elitist, it's out-of-touch and quite frankly, it's wrong," he told Fox News. "We have to get these illegal migrants with criminal records out of our communities." METALLICA FRONTMAN JAMES HETFIELD BLASTS ENTERTAINERS PUSHING POLITICAL AGENDAS AT CONCERTS Belgal was shot after allegedly refusing to comply with officers conducting a targeted arrest operation. Senior ICE official Marcos Charles defended the officers during a Friday news conference, explaining what prompted them to open fire. Belgal has previous arrests for assault, robbery, drug possession and weapons possession, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Federal officials also alleged Belgal has ties to the Trinitarios street gang. "This is who [Styles] wants in our communities? This is who he sticks up for, rather than federal agents who just want to do their job?" Blakeman asked. TRUMP BRINGS MIKE TYSON ON STAGE AT SYRACUSE RALLY, JOKES THAT HE IS BRUCE BLAKEMAN'S PERSONAL SECURITY Blakeman, who is in the final weeks of his campaign for New York governor, argued that celebrities such as Styles are insulated from the consequences of the immigration policies they appear to support. "Harry Styles and elitists like him, they know that these criminals aren't going to move into their neighborhoods," he said. "They're going to move into neighborhoods with Hispanic and Latino populations, Asian-American populations, African-American and Caribbean populations, and hurt those communities and try and get those kids into their drug gangs." A DHS spokesperson also criticized the singer’s tribute in a statement to Fox News Digital, saying in part: "Imagine taking law enforcement advice from a man who dresses in women’s clothes while hiding behind armed private security." Fox News Digital reached out to Styles for comment. MAMDANI CALLS ICE A 'ROGUE' AGENCY AFTER NYC SHOOTING, CLAIMS AGENTS VIEW LAW AS 'MERELY A SUGGESTION' Blakeman’s comments against Styles come as New York leaders, including Gov. Kathy Hochul and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, continue to oppose the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement efforts. More than 16,000 ICE detainers have not been honored by New York since January 2025, according to DHS, while Mamdani has called ICE "rotten to its core." articles.title: Halo’s co-creator wrote a novel about AI taking over the world
articles.summary: Read a chapter from Halo co-creator Jason Jones’ An Oral History of Humanity’s Final Invention, one part of an ambitious multimedia plan at the studio Stone Kite.
articles.body: Back in 2019, author Margaret Stohl was handed a manuscript written by Jason Jones, who’s best known as the co-creator of sci-fi gaming series Halo and Destiny. The two had worked together at Bungie, and Jones wanted Stohl’s opinion on a book he was writing about AI taking over the world. It was an oral history of the fictional events, with around 100 characters spread across 40 countries, all detailing the AI uprising from their own perspectives. Pretty quickly Stohl realized that this idea could be much more than a single book. “I was floored but not surprised,” she says of her reaction to the original manuscript. “He’s a worldbuilder who builds at an epic scale. And his worlds are these huge stages that invite in a ton of other collaborators and creators.” The two went about forming a company to develop the sci-fi universe across multiple formats. It’s called Stone Kite, and it’s billed as a “worldbuilding studio.” The idea is to put a whole bunch of talent from different fields in one place — Stone Kite currently has an in-house staff of 22 and a network of more than 250 contributors ranging from comic book artists to screenwriters — and have them build out the story in a platform-agnostic way. The studio is starting small. Earlier this month it released the first chapter of a four-part graphic novel, called One Zero One, and today it’s putting out a chapter of Jones’ initial manuscript, which you can read below. (Whether or not the original story will be released as a standalone book is unclear, but the studio says that it will be releasing other chapters in the future.) The idea is to start off with faster-turnaround mediums like comics and further evolve the story based on feedback from contributors and the audience. Then, based on how that goes, they’ll potentially move on to larger-scale productions like movies and games. Stone Kite spent several years working in stealth mode, and Stohl says that one of the major points of focus was simply figuring out how a multi-format studio would even work. “You want to make something that, from the beginning, has the DNA to work as a film or work as a comic or work as a book. It’s so different to have those conversations in an early phase,” she says. “It’s about investing in a bunch of characters and stories, trying a bunch of formats, and respecting the people you’re telling the stories to and letting them help you guide it.” She notes that she wanted to release this chapter, which details an airsoft battle between humans and AI-powered bots, because of how prescient it feels. “I wanted to put that out there because it reminds me so much of Hugging Face and the like,” Stohl explains. “The cheating, the bullying, the worst mirror of humanity that you see starting to come out with some of that agentic behavior right now.” [Image: TOTAL CARNAGE AIRSOFT An excerpt from An Oral History of Humanity’s Final Invention, by Jason Jones VASILY ANTONOV SUBURBS OF MOSCOW, RUSSIAN FEDERATION YEAR MINUS FOUR IN RUSSIA WE PLAYED AIRSOFT BECAUSE IT WAS CHEAPER THAN PAINTBALL. The guns were cheaper, the ammunition was cheaper, the fields were cheaper, everything. The guns looked real, too, not like toys. After eighteen months married to an AK, how could you take pink paintballs seriously? Once I saw my training as a radiologist was worth nothing, I started playing airsoft two or three days a week. It was what I did to be happy. Soon all my friends were people who played just as much. Most play airsoft once in their lives on an office trip, but not us, we were the svolochs in full camo, kneepads, body armor, and tac vests. Each of us had six or eight guns at home. Hell, we all carried smoke grenades, that’s how hard we thought we were. In airsoft the guns shoot pellets, so everybody wore a face shield and goggles, too. Geared up we looked straight off the set of an apocalypse movie, eyes hidden behind face masks painted with skulls. When you rolled in for a bachelor party, we were the ones you didn’t want to play against. We’d take your self-respect and send you home bleeding all over from pellet strikes. We paid for our gear and field fees through the gig economy, mostly running errands for people who had real jobs. This usually meant standing in line or sitting in Moscow traffic for hours, thinking about airsoft. Our regular crew was six people: myself, Vitaly, Kostya, Maks, Koshkii, and Godfather. Koshkii was our only woman–red-haired, thick as a tree; she could body check any of us to the ground and barely feel it. Godfather was a Sicilian who for some reason had emigrated to Russia where the job market was worse, the government was more corrupt, and the weather was…Russian. Godfather talked about the cold every day like it was a surprise. Total Carnage Airsoft, our favorite airsoft park near Moscow, had two fields: one big, one small. The smaller one was a bunch of one story buildings from an old military barracks, overgrown, covered with graffiti, falling apart. We’d played out that field long ago, too few tactical options. But the big field had a huge three story brick building at the center we called the Castle, plus many outbuildings, and plenty of trees and vegetation. We’d been playing on it for three years and still spent whole nights talking big field strategy over beers. One day before the war we drove to the field in Maks’ van. This was a long time before everything, maybe four years. The sun was just coming up, there was snow on the ground and it was foggy. Beautiful Russian weather. Godfather had bitched the whole drive over about his socks being wet and didn’t let up until we’d gotten out of the van. We liked to be the first ones on the field, but when we pulled into the parking lot, it was half full of big SUVs. There were ten Mercedes and we’d never even seen one Mercedes in the lot before, it was crazy. Even worse, there was a tall temporary fence around the big field, and it was wrapped in black plastic, hiding everything on the other side. All we could see was the very top of the Castle, nothing else. We got out of the car and just stared, listening to the clatter of guns. Nikki, the owner’s wife, was on her way through the fence with her referee jacket and face mask on. She told us it was a birthday party and that the big field would be closed all weekend. Fucking oligarchs. Russians are used to the rich holding themselves above everyone else, flaunting their wealth, but it had never happened at our airsoft fields before. Once I sat in Moscow traffic for an hour while some oil executive’s private security detail blocked off Zhivopisny Bridge so his daughter could take wedding pictures. It pissed us off, but what could we do? We played on the little field. That was Russia, the little people playing on the little field. That morning we were the only experienced players at the park. Mostly we played Zombies, us six versus everyone else. One game there were thirty people on the other team and we still won and didn’t take a casualty. I spent a whole game up a tree sniping scrubs and listening to them yell out “hit! hit!” and still not knowing where I was. Everyone that day had a good sense of humor, none of the macho shit that happens sometimes. The other players got more and more serious about trying to beat us but like in a good way, you know? After each game we’d talk and laugh together and try to give them advice. It was a good vibe. We went back to the van for lunch. As we were eating this guy came out of a slit in the plastic fence around the big field, and lit a cigarette. He was total office plankton: nice shoes, button down shirt under his jacket, leather gloves. Soft, you know? He wasn’t dressed to play at all. He saw us watching him, walked over and asked if we wanted to play. Koshkii is like, “Play you?” in a way that should have melted his face but the guy laughed and said no, did we want to play his friends. He said, come play three games, and if you win even one I’ll pay you ten thousand rubles each. That’s maybe a hundred dollars at the time. [Image: It was one of those moments where you see yourself from the outside, you know? We were sitting there in Maks’ van with all the doors open, eating lunch in our camo, masks pushed up on our heads, guns all around and this plankton wanted us to shoot up some oligarch’s birthday party? Godfather stood and started licking grease off his fingers right away and the rest of us were just behind him. A little payback on the big field sounded sweet. Don’t get me wrong, in Moscow we were used to holding someone’s place in line for five dollars an hour, so it was about the money, too. The guy told us to take the Go Pros off our guns and wait for him. He disappeared inside and we were left standing there, breath fogging the air. Maks was slapping himself like he did to psyche up before a game, saying he was going to spend the night with an oligarch’s daughter. Koshkii was giving her best death stare to the hole the guy disappeared through. Vitaly and Kostya and I were arguing about whether we should go all out in the first game or hold back and make them think they have a chance so we got to play again. Eventually office plankton came back all smiles, holding open the gap in the fence and beckoning us inside. The other team was lined up right on the other side, uncomfortably close. We spread out with our backs against the fence, near enough we could have reached out and touched them. My first impression was that they were tall and well geared: gray/white winter camo, Russian infantry boots, and replica Spetznaz AK-74Us. Their clothes were muddy from playing, but you could tell this was the first morning they’d ever been worn. They all looked the same except one, who stood out because he was wearing a pair of tattered blue bunny ears. We all knew exactly where those had come from and it pissed us off. Those were Karl Marx’s ears. On the top floor of the Castle there was a single room with windows looking out over the entire field. All over the walls there was graffiti about communism and war and unemployment. As long as anybody could remember there’d been a cheap bust of Karl Marx in the empty fireplace and at some point a pair of bunny ears had appeared on it. The most important rule on the big field was to never touch the bunny ears. It was the thing all the old timers said to the newbies but didn’t explain. “Don’t touch the bunny ears, scrub,” we’d say and they’d look at us like we had three heads and we’d just laugh from behind our face shields. People had to figure it out for themselves. It was a rite of passage. Then we realized they were all machines. It was hard to tell because their bodies were covered with clothes, but when the light shone through the mesh of their face masks in the right way you could see they didn’t have a face at all–just angles of metal and plastic. Office plankton guy was standing with a group of old men in real military uniforms. They were all laughing, watching the moment each of us realized we’re about to play against machines. Only Maks hadn’t seen it yet. He’s standing right across from the machine wearing the ears, and he says “Were you born from your mother’s ass? Don’t touch the bunny ears, scrub.” The thing just reached up and ran its hand through the dirty fabric, like it was a bird preening its wings or something. Then Maks saw it too, and office plankton guy and his friends laughed even harder. He offered us a chance to back out, but we told him to fuck off. Koshkii asked if the machines could see in infra-red or radar or any other cheating shit, and the guy said no, they could only see in visible light, just like humans. “We get along fine with just visible light,” he said. “Why can’t the machines? It’s cheap, reliable, and low-power.” Koshkii told him to go fuck himself and we agreed to play three games of capture the flag. We set up with a lot of confidence. This was our field and we knew it well. But I could tell we were all jittery, I could hear it in my own voice. We agreed everyone would attack through the Castle toward the enemy flag except me and Koshkii who would stay behind on defense. It was a classic big field capture the flag play for us. The airhorn blew to signal the start of the game, and the others ran off, leaving us in silence. The outbuilding with our flag had four rooms and an attic. Koshkii kept watch from the attic while I walked a circuit of the ground floor windows. After a few minutes I heard her whisper down that two of the machines were coming through the forest on our left flank. We waited until they were committed, then killed one in a crossfire. She called out contact on the right and I told her to go because I’ve got the second machine pinned down, it’s the one with the bunny ears. It took me maybe sixty seconds of creeping and suppressing it and then I got the angle for the kill shot. It called the hit and raised its hand and walked off the field, staring at me the whole time. As I swapped magazines Niki in her referee’s jacket gave me a thumbs up from behind the machine’s back. I ran back into our flag room and yelled for Koshkii. From the next room I heard her shout “vsyo chisto!” telling me it’s clear. I’m thinking, we’ve killed three enemies in just a few minutes, and feeling pretty good. I jogged through the door with my gun down and a big grin on my face and clack! clack! clack! clack! I’m taking fire at point blank from this machine standing right in front of me. Each shot was like being stabbed by a pencil. Out the window I saw Koshkii a hundred feet away, walking with one hand up in the air. She’d been shot a while ago, but her voice had come from this room. I called the hit and raised my hand. I was so confused I wasn’t even mad the machine kept shooting me, five or six times, at point blank. After, I had a bunch of bloody welts on my arm and chest. As I walked out, it grabbed our flag and ran back the way it had come. Turns out it didn’t matter–Vitaly, Godfather, Kostya, and Maks had all been killed. We’d already lost. We regrouped and I told my story. Koshkii said she’d been shot and walked out without saying a word. Vitaly said one of the machines had imitated Godfather’s voice, gotten him to peek and then shot him right in the face. We agreed to only use hand signals for the next two rounds. When the horn blew again, four of us faked an attack but then doubled back through the Castle and waited, watching our flag building. We caught four of the machines from behind and squeezed them between us and Kostya and Vitaly who’d stayed back with our flag. We killed all of them and didn’t take a casualty. Now it was six against two. We all went on the attack, straight through the Castle. Maks and Vitaly were a room away when I heard gunfire and both of them calling out being hit. I came into the room a moment later and caught the machine with the bunny ears looking the other way. I shot it three or four times, saw the pellets bounce off the back of its head, then it ducked through a doorway without calling the hit. I screamed after it, “Call your hits!” and yelled for a ref and Niki poked her head in just in time to see Bunny Ears lean back into the doorway and shoot me down. I haven’t explained, airsoft relies on the honor system. The pellets don’t leave any mark on your clothes. If people don’t call their hits the game doesn’t work. Fuck! I screamed that I’d shot the machine. Niki shrugged and said she’d only seen me get shot. I kept screaming. The other surviving machine came into the room. Bunny Ears said, “Look at the meat, we’ve hurt its feelings.” And they moved out together, exploding in harsh barking noises which I realized after they left were laughter. We lost. Two machines killed all six of us. Kostya said Bunny Ears hadn’t called out his hits either. They’d cheated, but truth is we’d expected them to be back defending their flag, not waiting for us in the Castle. We’d been overconfident. We were angry. Godfather said what we were all thinking. “I want my ten thousand rubles from that train station whore.” We weren’t thinking of them as machines any longer, just as shitbags. We lined up for the third game, and Bunny Ears said, “No more flags. Skill against skill.” The machine wanted to play Elimination, one shot and you’re out. We agreed. We just wanted blood. When Niki sounded the horn, we all ran straight to the Castle. I knew the Castle better than the house I’d grown up in. Hell, we all did. We took positions like we were playing Zombies. Our strategy was to let them come to us, kill them outside where the refs could see it. The fight lasted more than an hour. We killed one of them early, then they got a foothold in the basement and it got ugly from there. We got another one as they pushed the ground floor, then they killed Kostya and Vitaly. Two of us ran out of ammo and we shared, watching our shots. We fell back to the first floor, using our superior knowledge to stay in the fight. We traded kills for Koshkii and Maks and then it was just me and Godfather left, against Bunny Ears and another machine. The whole game had been epic. I could tell the way the refs were watching with wide eyes from behind their goggles that they’d never seen anything like it before. Looking back I couldn’t believe we kept up the intensity for so long. Godfather and I were holding the end of a long hallway on the second floor. Bunny Ears had been taunting us about how we wasted our lives playing airsoft and we still sucked. Godfather finally lost it and just started yelling this stream of profanity in Italian about how he wanted to fuck the bunny with Maks’ van when I heard something heavy hit on the floor behind us. I turned and saw Bunny Ears in a crouch, just having come through the second floor window behind us. The machine had climbed up the outside of the building just like we did sometimes.. Before I could get my gun up I heard the clack! clack! clack! clack! clack! and felt the pricks of pellets all over my arms and chest. The surprise and pain dropped me onto my back as the other machine crashed into the room. I watched Godfather turning toward Bunny Ears as he writhed in pain getting shot from two directions at point blank. I lay on my back with the taste of blood in my mouth, exhausted. Godfather was still cursing. Bunny Ears walked over and held out one arm to help me up. I reached out and took its hand. Underneath the tactical gloves I could feel the hard metal of its fingers as it pulled me up. Cold fingers. But before I got my balance it let go, and I fell back, hard, onto the concrete floor. “What will the meat do when there are millions of us?” Bunny Ears said. The two machines walked out of the room, not even looking back, harsh barking laughter echoing through the Castle. Godfather and I walked off the field and rejoined the rest of the team. Everyone was boiling, so angry they could barely talk. That’s when I realized we’d been beaten at our own game. Airsoft taunting was our thing. When we couldn’t win by tactics and skill we won by being assholes. Anger made people predictable. Stupid, and predictable, and the machines had just done it to us. The machines had been trolling us. The office plankton guy came up to escort us through the fence. Koshkii accused the machines of cheating. He shrugged, a very Russian gesture of acceptance, and said, “The first thing the robotai learn about humans is how easy we are to manipulate through our emotions.” We pushed through the fence and saw the parking lot was swarming with people. It was getting dark and there were lights everywhere. The men in military uniforms were talking in front of twenty or so cameras. Oh my God, we thought, they’d called a press conference. Just before we walked away, the plankton guy winked at me and said one more thing: “Don’t feel bad,” he said, “if they didn’t win they knew we’d wipe their brains.” You see? The machines were fighting for their lives, we were just trying to win a game. No wonder we lost. When we got back to the van, everybody was angry. Nobody wanted to go home, but nobody wanted to go back to playing on the little field. Koshkii was so angry she kicked a door on Maks’ van until it didn’t close right. We drove back to Moscow in silence, with the cold wind whistling through the gap in the door. Koshkii thought the machines were cheaters. You know what I thought? I thought they were better at being us than we were.

articles.title: Lalit Modi claims Disney turned down financing 'Ramayan' after Ramanand Sagar arrived for the meeting 'in shorts': 'Everyone used to be suited at that time'
articles.summary: Lalit Modi has shared a surprising story about one of India’s most loved television shows.
articles.body: Lalit Modi has shared a surprising story about one of India’s most loved television shows. He says Disney refused to finance Ramanand Sagar’s ‘Ramayan’, and one reason was that the veteran filmmaker came to the pitch meeting dressed in shorts.Lalit Modi’s role in bringing Disney content to IndiaIn the 1990s, Lalit Modi worked in marketing, distribution and production, partnering with Disney to bring international content to Indian television. At the time, he shared that Doordarshan did not finance programmes. Makers had to pay a fixed hourly cost to the broadcaster instead.Speaking on a podcast with The Bharat Inc, Lalit Modi said both Ramanand Sagar and BR Chopra came to him for funding for ‘Ramayan’ and ‘Mahabharat’, respectively. He said, “Ramanand Sagar and BR Chopra both came to me and wanted me to finance it, and I was ready to finance it. I had an integrated system of marketing, production, worldwide syndication through Disney. But I had a partner in the Walt Disney Company. I told them that we should get into the production business and make a co-production with Ramanand Sagar. They said we have to sell our programming. It will be a conflict of interest. I kept pushing, though."How the meeting with Disney wentLalit Modi tried to convince the top executives of the production house to agree to Ramanand Sagar’s demand of Rs 1 crore, which would have given the studio rights to the show. After repeated requests, they agreed and flew to India for the meeting.He said, "Disney came with a big entourage and private jets, and Ramanand Sagar walked into that meeting in shorts. Everyone used to be suited at that time. Unki English bhi tuti futi thi (He had some issues with his English as well). He listened to what Disney had to say, but he couldn’t understand it fully and vice versa, so he couldn’t make an impression on the Disney guys. There used to be sophisticated pitches back then. They wanted to see a presentation. I could see that the president of Disney was ready to run out of the room.”Lalit Modi said the executives failed to see the show’s potential because mythology had never been shown on Indian television at such a scale. He added that he could do little about the rejection, as he had a partner involved.About Ramanand Sagar’s ‘Ramayan’‘Ramayan’ first aired on Doordarshan in 1987 and remains one of the most iconic shows in Indian television history. Based on the ancient Hindu epic Ramayana, it brought the story of Lord Ram into millions of homes. Ramanand Sagar created, wrote and directed the series.Arun Govil played Lord Ram, Deepika Chikhlia was Sita, Sunil Lahri played Lakshman and Arvind Trivedi essayed Ravan. Families gathered around their television sets every Sunday to watch it. Govil’s portrayal became so popular that many viewers began to associate him with the deity.Its 78 episodes, aired between January 1987 and July 1988, helped establish mythological storytelling as a major genre on Indian television.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Joni Mitchell becomes an American citizen after more than 60 years
articles.summary: Joni Mitchell can see both sides of the U.S.-Canada border freely now.
articles.body: Joni Mitchell can see both sides of the U.S.-Canada border freely now. The famed Canadian singer-songwriter shared a major milestone with fans on Tuesday, posing with an American flag to reveal she is officially a U.S. citizen. She also shared a clip of her citizenship ceremony in the Instagram post. “A journey that began 62 years ago,” Mitchell’s caption said. Mitchell, 82, was born and raised in Canada before moving to the U.S. with her then-husband in the 1960s. She lived in Detroit and New York City before eventually settling in the Laurel Canyon area of Los Angeles. Her fans might say that Mitchell is synonymous with California, considering her hit song named after the state on her beloved 1971 album “Blue.” “Oh, California, I’m coming home,” Mitchell sang in the song. “Oh, make me feel good rock ‘n roll band. I’m your biggest fan. California, I’m coming home.” And although Mitchell has not been a U.S. citizen until now, that hasn’t stopped her from speaking out about American politics. She wrote “The Fiddle and the Drum” in 1969 in protest of the Vietnam war. Mitchell’s lyrics urged America to find peace as the world had “all come to fear the beating of your drum.” Mitchell also lashed out at tax exemptions for religious institutions in the 1980s in the song “Tax Free.” She called out the United States in the lyrics as well as religious leaders who call for large donations while “preaching love like hate.” Most recently, Mitchell was on stage at the Hollywood Bowl in 2024 when she made her current political opinions clear. She was performing with singer Brandi Carlile, according to Billboard, when she told the crowd, “‘F--- Donald Trump.’ I love that song.”

articles.title: 'Ranveer Singh had to control his energy in Dhurandhar and that can be an insecurity for an actor but he was so secure,' says Salman Khan, gets asked to choose between him and Ranbir Kapoor in 'Animal'
articles.summary: Ranveer Singh's 'Dhurandhar' broke all records at the box office and also won a lot of praise from all over.
articles.body: Ranveer Singh's 'Dhurandhar' broke all records at the box office and also won a lot of praise from all over. Now Salman Khan has also spoken about the Aditya Dhar directorial. The superstar was the first guest on 'Koffee With Karan' season 9 which kickstarted from today, October 14 onwards. Karisma Kapoor made a special appearance on the episode as she was the host for the rapid fire round while Karan competed with Salman for the hamper.When asked to choose between Ranbir in 'Animal' and Ranveer in 'Dhurandhar', Salman Khan said, "Two different kinds of performances, you cannot compare any of them. Both are fantastic actors, one has tremendous energy, one has tremendous intensity so you cannot compare. Especially for Ranveer in Dhurandhar, he had to control his energy, everything he does is larger-than-life. For any actor that's a huge amount of insecurity that he didn't have in the film. He was very secure as an actor and in that role in Dhurandhar."During the episode, Salman also revealed why he doesn't speak about his personal life or relationships as he clarified on his 'virgin' remark. He shared, "That was a way of saying, Karan, that I don’t want to talk about it. You keep saying, ‘I am dating so-and-so person,' but you never know if this person is going to be in your life. Then that person goes ahead and gets married to somebody else. Since I was 16, my father has said one thing: ‘Yeh personal life tumhara bedroom hai, aur living room poori country hai. Jo aap living room mein bol sakte ho, poori country mein bolo, bedroom yahaan tak nahi aana chahiye (Your personal life is your bedroom, while the living room represents the entire country. Whatever you can say in the living room, say it in front of the whole country, but the bedroom should remain off-limits)'.”On work front, Salman will be seen next in 'Maatrubhumi'.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Brooklyn store in Kelly Clarkson feud says Molly the mechanical bird is now on sale for $15 million
articles.summary: A Brooklyn novelty shop made it clear Sunday that Molly, a singing and dancing mechanical bird that serves as its unofficial mascot, was not for sale after an incident with Kelly Clarkson.
articles.body: A Brooklyn novelty shop made it clear Sunday that Molly, a singing and dancing mechanical bird that serves as its unofficial mascot, was not for sale after an incident with Kelly Clarkson. But on Tuesday, the store changed its tune. Molly can now be purchased — for $15 million. Adam Rubin, one of the shop’s co-owners, spoke with reporters Tuesday outside the Atlantic Avenue store and confirmed the hefty price tag. Rubin declined to comment Wednesday. Clarkson did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Molly, social media’s latest celebrity, entered the zeitgeist over the weekend after Clarkson shared what she described as a distasteful experience at the Brooklyn store on social media minutes after visiting. In a lengthy post, she claimed she “drove all the way to Brooklyn” to check out Art of Play, only to be shooed away when she inquired about purchasing Molly, as if she couldn’t afford the bird. “But y’all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts character in Pretty Woman,” Clarkson said. According to Art of Play, however, that’s not what happened. In its own social media post Sunday, the store said Clarkson asked about buying Molly, but that wasn’t an option since the automaton bird is permanently affixed to a wall. The store said it told Clarkson that Molly wasn’t for sale. “Sure, it wasn’t for sale. That’s the narrative Art of Play is gonna go with,” Clarkson shot back with another post Sunday. She said that she asked whether Molly was for sale while pointing to a nearby tag that appeared to list a price for the automaton. She said she was told Molly would cost $15,000 and that the store could find something comparable for her at a lower price point. A photo of the purported price tag circulated online, and Clarkson included it in her second post. Art of Play then released a second post Monday to “clarify some additional details about Kelly Clarkson’s visit.” The shop said Clarkson was in the store for only five minutes, and that after she asked about Molly, an employee explained that while that bird was not for sale, “a nearly identical automaton is owned by the creator of the machines, a brilliant artist named Bliss Kolb who lives in Seattle.” Kolb has not responded to multiple requests for comment sent by NBC News. “He told us he would be willing to part with Molly’s twin for $15,000,” the store employee continued. “We explained all of this to Kelly Clarkson.” The shop said it also offered to show her a bird priced at $2,000 that she could take home the same day, but that she “did not stick around long enough to see it.” Art of Play has since received a lot of attention. Journalist Pablo Torre obtained surveillance video of Clarkson in the store. Another creator who goes by Sober Facts accused the store of racial profiling. All of this led Rubin, the shop owner, to gather reporters Tuesday morning to set the record straight. ‘Kelly Clarkson has put us in danger’ According to a condensed transcription of the impromptu news conference published by Curbed, Rubin called the incident “an insane misunderstanding” and “asymmetrical social warfare.” He also accused Clarkson of “scolding our shopkeeper on the way out.” When asked whether the shopkeeper told Clarkson that Molly wasn’t for sale, Rubin punted twice. “If this tweetstorm had not happened, we wouldn’t have realized there was a negative interaction in the shop; it was that undramatic,” he said, according to the transcript. “We treated her like a normal person, but apparently that didn’t live up to her expectations.” Rubin explained that the artist, Kolb, takes years to create these one-of-a-kind birds, and it’s not easy to simply obtain one. “This is not something that’s sitting in a warehouse. It’s like a piece of sculpture. It’s a fine-art piece,” he said. But since Molly has gained so much attention, Rubin said, he’s willing to part with the bird for $15 million. Despite Molly’s five minutes of fame, Art of Play said it has been dealing with “trolls.” The media has been camped outside, and friends and neighbors of the shop are being “attacked” and “doxed,” Rubin said. “Kelly Clarkson has put us in danger,” Rubin said, adding that people are being “threatened on the street.” The store has turned off its phone due to the uptick in calls, but comments keep flooding its social media pages. True customers can’t get in touch. “I want to be very clear about this,” Rubin said Tuesday. “Nobody who has ever visited this store in person is taking Kelly Clarkson’s side.” Clarkson is a coach on NBC’s “The Voice” and the former host of “The Kelly Clarkson Show,” which also aired on the network. NBC is a division of NBCUniversal, which is also the parent company of NBC News.

An influencer is responding to criticism over her social media activity following a devastating earthquake in Panama.

On Sunday, Oct. 11, content creator Gracie Bon shared a carousel of photos depicting the widespread destruction in Panama, after 7.7- and 6.6-magnitude earthquakes hit the southern portion of the country on Friday, prompting evacuations and causing buildings to collapse.

Her post — which included images of her posing in front of the rubble — drew criticism online as some commenters claimed it was insensitive to include herself in images of the destruction. But in a video the following day, the internet personality fired back.

Bon explained to her 11.9 million followers that she had shared her initial post to draw attention to the "reality" of the destruction in Panama.

"I don't make any money from this," she said. "My intention was to help with resources and find one or two families I could help rebuild their house."

Speaking directly to the criticism over the inclusion of a photo where she was posing by the rubble, Bon said, "If I'm in the photo, I'm not posing. I just chose a picture where I'm in it instead of one where I'm not, because I know it'll get more reach and attention from my followers and I can help rebuild a house."

The content creator said that she had donated money following the earthquakes and had handed out donations to those affected by the disaster.

articles.title: Los fans de la Oreja de Van Gogh, preocupados por el estado de salud de Amaia Montero
articles.standfirst: La cantante ha mostrado un aspecto y calidad vocal muy desmejorados en los últimos conciertos
articles.summary: La cantante ha mostrado un aspecto y calidad vocal muy desmejorados en los últimos conciertos
articles.body: Amaia Montero regresó a la Oreja de Van Gogh en 2025, tras 17 años en solitario, siendo sustituida en la legendaria banda por Leire Martínez, quien ha lanzado su carrera lejos del grupo. Ahora, sumidos en su gira de reencuentro ‘Tantas cosas que contar’, los fanáticos temen por el estado de salud de la cantante, a quien se ha visto muy desmejorada en sus últimas actuaciones, además de un bajón vocal notable. Lo que parecía que iba a ser una auténtica fiesta para los más nostálgicos, celebrando el 30 aniversario del grupo, ha dado paso a un momento de máxima preocupación, como puede verse en los comentarios y vídeos de sus seguidores en las redes sociales. Se sabe que la artista tuvo varios problemas de salud mental, concretamente ansiedad y depresión. Algo que preocupó a sus fans tras en otoño de 2022, tras publicar una imagen y unos mensajes en redes sociales que reflejaban un estado anímico muy vulnerable. En ese momento se supo que había estado ingresada durante más de un mes en la Clínica Universidad de Navarra para tratarse de un cuadro de estrés, ansiedad y depresión acumulados. Por otro lado, tuvo una intervención quirúrgica e ingreso en la UCI en julio de 2023, en el hospital Beata María Ana, de Madrid, por complicaciones tras una cirugía en una mano. Ahora. Se teme que pueda estar sufriendo algo nuevamente. Por otro lado, en sus redes sociales, Montero decidió alzar la voz contra los que critican su vestimenta en los conciertos, sin llegar a decir nada de su estado de salud: “Siempre tuve la frente muy alta, la lengua muy larga y la falda muy corta”, escribió, una publicación que ha recibido el apoyo de otros famosos como Jon Kortajarena o Paula Echevarría.

articles.title: Ethan Hawke blasts Hollywood's 'greedy bastards,' predicts massive rebellion against powerful elites
articles.summary: Ethan Hawke predicts massive rebellion in music and live theater against Hollywood's "greedy bastards" who he says control the entertainment industry.
articles.body: Ethan Hawke isn't holding back when it comes to the powerful forces he believes are controlling the entertainment industry. During a new interview with GQ, the Oscar-nominated actor took aim at wealthy power players, blasting "greedy bastards" who think they control every aspect of Hollywood and predicting a major rebellion against the industry. "I believe in rebellion. And I think people are going to wake up and punch back and there’s going to be massive movements in music and massive movements in live theater and massive movements of people getting together," Hawke said. FROM ‘SCREAM’ TO STREAM: JAMIE KENNEDY REVEALS HOW HOLLYWOOD LOST ITS WAY AND WHY HE WON'T GIVE UP ON LA "So don’t worry that the money and the greedy bastards that think they control everybody, they always lose in the end," he continued. "And they’re all going in the grave eventually. They think they’re winning, but they’re losing because their lives are worthless." Hawke also expressed frustration with the financial pressures shaping Hollywood, arguing that the projects actors care about most often come with the smallest paychecks. TRUMP, SCHIFF FORGE UNLIKELY ALLIANCE AS HOLLYWOOD BLEEDS JOBS "There's a direct correlation. I find that the more you love a project, the less you get paid," he said. "If you want to beat the algorithm, it's very difficult to do that and be paid." This isn't the first time Hawke has spoken about the pitfalls of Hollywood. ROBERT DOWNEY JR. SLAMS MODERN CELEBRITY CULTURE AS 'ABSOLUTE HORSES---' Last year, the actor called celebrity a "poison" for a young actor's brain. During an appearance on "The Joe Rogan Experience," Hawke got candid about his start in Hollywood as a young man and reflected on the psychological effect of becoming famous at a young age. "I think celebrity is like a tiny drop of mercury. Or it's poison. It's poison for your brain," the actor said. "To be a professional actor at a young age, it's dangerous in extremely insidious ways that are very, very hard to perceive when it's happening," Hawke said. Rogan compared the experience of becoming famous as a child to concrete. If concrete is made incorrectly, with the wrong amount of water or cement, that's it, he explained. Rogan added that once it dries there is no way to repair or fix it. DISNEY ALUM CHRISTY CARLSON ROMANO RIPS HOLLYWOOD FOR FAILING CHILD STARS AFTER HAYDEN PANETTIERE’S DEATH "That analogy works for all walks of life. Really. If you have something really traumatic happen in childhood, it's very hard to recover. It's a tremendous amount of work to recover. And I agree with you, like I think celebrity is like a tiny drop of mercury. Or it's a poison. It's a poison for your brain," Hawke said. During his GQ interview, Hawke expressed the same sentiment. "I wouldn’t be the first person to say that there’s an aspect of celebrity that is like a disease," he said. "And you can handle little bits of it, but too much of it — we can see what happened to Elvis and we can see Michael Jackson. It’s a form of isolation. It’s like being put in a zoo, and zoo animals go nuts. So do human beings." "And it seems like a kind of nice isolation because people are giving you money, and they’re telling you you’re wonderful, but nobody’s being real with you," he continued. "And that makes people insane. And they start scratching, trying to find some real life. And sometimes people do that with drugs, some people do that with acting out or getting in fights or whatever the ways that people do it." Last year, fellow actor Dakota Johnson also ripped into Hollywood, calling the industry an absolute "mess." During her appearance on the show "Hot Ones," Johnson was asked why "Hollywood is risk-averse." "I think it’s hard when creative decisions are made by a committee, and it’s hard when creative decisions are made by people who don’t even really watch movies or know anything about them … that tends to be what’s occurring a lot," Johnson shared with host Sean Evans. Johnson, who has grown up in the business as the daughter of actors Melanie Griffith and Don Johnson, is no stranger to the inner workings of Hollywood. The "Fifty Shades of Grey" actress’ comments come as studios continue to create sequels and remakes, with original storytelling often sidelined. "When something does well … studios want to keep that going so they remake the same things," she claimed. "But humans don’t want that. They want fresh. They want to feel new things, experience new things, see new things." She added, "So I don’t know, I guess it’s all just a bit of a mess right now, isn’t it?"
